title: Childhood and Education #21: Grades and Standards
author: Zvi Mowshowitz
summary: In this installment of his Childhood and Education series, Zvi Mowshowitz collects studies, posts and social-media threads on how students are admitted, graded and assessed, and adds his own commentary to each. He argues that objective measures such as the SAT help disadvantaged applicants, while holistic admissions reward wealthy families who can manufacture non-academic credentials and a staged personal story. He then turns to grade inflation, using Harvard's own report (about 60 percent of grades are now A's) to show how removing meaningful grading pushes students toward extracurricular competition and away from learning. He proposes a statistical alternative, Grade Average Above Par, that would compare performance across classes and schools. The later sections tie AI cheating, student disengagement and campus preference falsification to the same root problem: institutions have stopped convincing students that learning itself is valued. The piece is an opinionated curation rather than a single-thesis essay, but its through-line is that weak standards and weak incentives corrode both admissions and learning.
points: Mowshowitz holds that SAT-style objective tests reduce the advantage of high-income applicants, while holistic review, legacy preference and athletic recruitment amplify it without predicting better outcomes.
He suggests the real flaw of the SAT and ACT is the ceiling effect, and that harder, higher-ceiling tests would let top students separate themselves and give them something to aim at.
Harvard's grade inflation report is used as a case study in how removing real consequences for performance shifts student effort into extracurricular signalling and leaves academics feeling fake.
His Grade Average Above Par proposal would score each class against how a marginal admitted student would be expected to perform, making grades comparable across courses and schools.

Through the Clay Shirky and NYU examples, he frames AI cheating as a symptom: if an assignment's only value is compelling student effort, students who see no consequences will rationally skip the effort.
quotes: Holistic admissions creates incentives to look good by holistic standards, as teens scramble to optimize their every moment, including an increasing emphasis on eating everyone’s summers, to score every point they can and convey a ‘story’ to college admissions.
There is a very easy and obvious fix for that, which are academic credentials that do differentiate at that level. What, like it’s hard?
If you do holistic admissions, and people do something amazingly great, admit them.

As you would expect, you put the kids that won the competition to get into Harvard into Harvard, take away the competition for grades, and you get other competitions stepping up to fill the void, except now no one is focusing on the classes.
There should be no need to coddle unprepared students at Harvard, because there should be no need to ever admit an unprepared student.

Par performance is defined as how a marginal admitted student would perform, and we use standard sports-style statistical methods to compare high school and college grades to form predictions of that score for every class, based on who took the class and how those students perform elsewhere.
The assignment itself is a MacGuffin, with the shelf life of sour cream and an economic value that rounds to zero dollars. It is valuable only as a way to compel student effort and thought.
The actual central thing here is that everyone involved seems to have stopped pretending college is about learning or acquiring skills?
